title: The red wines on the exam
lead: The twelve red grapes the Court can pour at Certified level, grouped where they're related, with their exam regions and how each one shows up on the grid.

intro.title: OAK IS PART OF THE ANSWER
intro.text: The Court's red list sets oak and quality level for many wines. Read it as a set of clues before you taste.

sections.name: Pinot Noir and Gamay

lines.label: On the exam
lines.text: Pinot Noir from the Côte d'Or (Village or Premier Cru), California (Carneros, Sonoma, Central Coast) and Oregon's Willamette Valley. Gamay from Beaujolais, with carbonic maceration and no oak.

lines.label: On the grid
lines.text: Both are paler reds with red fruit, low tannin and bright acidity. Gamay brings the carbonic line; Burgundy brings earth.

know: Pinot Noir: Côte d'Or (Village or 1er), California, Willamette Valley.
Pinot: pale to medium ruby, red fruit, low tannin, high acidity.
Burgundy is earthy and floral; California riper; Oregon tarter.
Gamay: Beaujolais with carbonic maceration, no oak.
Carbonic: juicy fruit, low tannin, banana and candied notes.

Nebbiolo: high tannin and acid; garnet rim even young.
Nebbiolo markers: cherry, rose, leather, anise.

lines.text: Cabernet Franc from Chinon or Bourgueil, in the Loire. Merlot from Pomerol or Saint-Émilion, and from Napa or Sonoma with new oak.

lines.label: On the grid

mixups.why: Burgundy shows earth and floral notes; California is riper and lusher; Oregon sits closer to Burgundy.
Both tart and firm: Nebbiolo has rose and the higher tannin; Sangiovese has tomato, oregano and balsamic.
Grenache shows stewed strawberry, dried herbs and over 15% alcohol; Rioja shows dill and coconut from American oak.
Shiraz shows black pepper and sometimes eucalyptus; Malbec shows a magenta rim, plum, cocoa and softer acidity.

facts.fact: Certified red examinable wines: Cabernet Franc (Loire: Chinon / Bourgueil); Cabernet Sauvignon (Bordeaux: Haut-Medoc / Graves, new oak; California: Napa Valley / Sonoma County / Paso Robles, new oak); Gamay (Burgundy, Beaujolais, with carbonic maceration, no oak); Grenache (Rhone: Chateauneuf-du-Pape / Gigondas); Malbec (Argentina, Mendoza); Merlot (Bordeaux: Pomerol / Saint-Emilion; California: Napa Valley / Sonoma County, new oak); Nebbiolo (Piedmont: Barolo / Barbaresco).

Certified red examinable wines (continued): Pinot Noir (France, Cote d'Or, Village or Premier Cru only; California: Napa Valley (Carneros) / Sonoma County / Central Coast; Oregon: Willamette Valley); Sangiovese (Tuscany: Brunello di Montalcino / Chianti Classico); Syrah (Northern Rhone: Cote-Rotie / Saint-Joseph / Crozes-Hermitage; Australia: South Australia / Western Australia / Victoria, new oak); Tempranillo (Spain, Rioja, Reserva or Gran Reserva, American oak); Zinfandel (California: Napa Valley / Sonoma County, new oak).
Expected skill set of a Certified Sommelier: 'Deductive Tasting Method ability for core classic red and white varieties'.

Red comparisons the Court suggests: Burgundy and US Pinot Noir; Burgundy Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo; Sangiovese and Nebbiolo; Sangiovese and Rioja; French Grenache and Rioja; Bordeaux and California Cabernet Sauvignon; Australian Shiraz, Argentine Malbec and California Zinfandel.

Red grid: color Purple, Ruby, Garnet; fruit lines Red, Black, Blue; non-fruit lines include Dried Herbs, Mint/Eucalyptus, Black Peppercorn, Coffee/Cocoa, Meat/Leather, Balsamic/Tar, Carbonic Maceration, Earth, Mineral, New Oak (Vanilla, Smoke, Toast, Coconut, Dill); structure Tannin, Acidity, Alcohol; red age ranges 1-3, 4-6, 7+ years.

Example red grid in the exam guide: fruit lines filled with blueberry, blackberry and black cherry; grape reasons 'black fruit, black pepper, eucalyptus'; climate reasons 'high alcohol, very ripe fruit'; country Australia; sales pitch mentions black cherry and black pepper with grilled beef or lamb.
Some regions classically blur the line of Old v. New World. 'Pumped up' red Burgundy: warm vintage gives riper fruit, medium-plus alcohol, oak more forward, too youthful for earth to show.

Original Napa Cabernet: pyrazines, moderate-plus alcohol and astringent tannins, fruit just ripe, oak not as forward. Modern: pyrazines more subtle, high alcohol, rounder tannins, overripe/liqueur-like fruit, oak more forward.
Wayne Belding, MS (quoted): Argentine Malbec and Aussie Shiraz rose from non-existent to classic in a few decades.
Nebbiolo and Grenache often show a garnet or orange rim even when young; Malbec often has a magenta rim.
Oak lactone gives woody, dill and coconut notes; European oak has been suggested to impart less oak lactone than American oak.
Court grape profile, Pinot Noir: climates cool, moderate, warm; possible whole cluster, neutral or new oak; top regions Burgundy, California, Oregon, New Zealand; color pale ruby to deep ruby.

Pinot Noir: primary flavors raspberry, cherry, mushroom, vanilla, hibiscus; pale to medium color from thin skins; red fruits with earthiness and spice; mushroom and leather with age; light to medium body, low tannins, high (medium-high) acidity, 12-14% ABV.

Burgundian Pinot Noir is more earthy and floral. California Pinot Noir is bigger, lusher and more fruit-forward: black cherry, black raspberry, vanilla, clove, cola. Oregon Pinot Noir is usually lighter and more tart (cranberry, Bing cherry, sometimes truffle) and often closest in style to Burgundy.
Court: Willamette Valley is cool Mediterranean with maritime influence; the Coast Range to the west creates a rain shadow.
Gamay: primary flavors pomegranate, blackberry bramble, violet, potting soil, peony; dry, medium-light body, very low tannin, medium-high acidity, 10-11.5% ABV.

Beaujolais is mostly made by semi-carbonic maceration, responsible for banana, candied fruit, pear, raspberry and cranberry aromas; Beaujolais has high acidity and low tannin; the 10 crus are all in the north, on mostly granite and schist.
Carbonic maceration: uncrushed grapes in a sealed vat topped with CO2; wines have low tannin and color, juicy fruit and bold yeast aromas.
Beaujolais: 13,500 ha in 12 AOCs, almost all Gamay (97%); the 10 crus include Morgon, Fleurie and Moulin-a-Vent.
Court grape profile, Nebbiolo: climates moderate, warm; tannin and acidity both high; possible large barrel and extended skin maceration; color medium ruby, deep ruby, garnet.
Nebbiolo: primary flavors cherry, rose, leather, anise, clay pot; bone-dry, medium-full body, high tannins, medium-high acidity, 13.5-15% ABV; delicate aromas with strong tannins.
Court (Certified column): Barolo 38 months total aging with at least 18 months in oak; Barbaresco 26 months with at least 9 in oak.
Barolo has a full, intense garnet color and elegant, complex tannins.
Court grape profile, Sangiovese: climates warm, hot; large barrel, neutral oak, blending; top region Tuscany (Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino); color pale ruby, deep ruby, garnet.
Sangiovese: primary flavors cherry, roasted tomato, sweet balsamic, oregano, espresso; bone-dry, medium-full body, medium-high tannins, medium-high acidity, 13.5-15% ABV.
Court (Certified column): Brunello is 100% Brunello (Sangiovese); Chianti Classico at least 80% Sangiovese.
Brunello di Montalcino: 2 years in oak and 4 months in bottle; released no earlier than 1 January of the fifth year after harvest.
Chianti Classico Annata: at least 80% Sangiovese, at least 12 months aging; Riserva at least 24 months.
Court grape profile, Grenache: climates warm, hot; styles fruity, unoaked, ripe, spicy; large barrel, blending, whole cluster; top regions Southern Rhone, Spain, Australia; color medium to deep ruby.

Grenache: primary flavors stewed strawberry, grilled plum, leather, dried herbs, blood orange; dry, medium-full body, medium tannins, medium acidity, over 15% ABV; championed in the Southern Rhone, roots in northeastern Spain.
Northern Rhone reds are Syrah; the Southern Rhone makes Grenache-based blends such as Chateauneuf-du-Pape.
Chateauneuf-du-Pape: Mediterranean climate with the Mistral, under 650 mm of rain and about 2,800 hours of sunshine; soils of rolled pebbles with red clay, sand and sandstone.
Court grape profile, Tempranillo: climates warm, hot; blending, large barrel, neutral and new oak; top regions Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Toro; color moderate ruby, deep ruby, garnet.

Tempranillo: primary flavors cherry, dried fig, cedar, tobacco, dill; dry, medium-full body, medium-high tannins, medium-high acidity, 13.5-15% ABV; thin skins, medium ruby to garnet color. Rioja tasting notes: cherry, dill, cigar box, sun-dried tomato, vanilla. With 10-20 years, dried fruit, nut and spice aromas develop.

Court: Rioja is continental, in a Cantabrian rain shadow along the Ebro, and traditionally aged in American oak. Certified column: Rioja Reserva at least 3 years with 1 in oak; Gran Reserva at least 5 years with 2 in oak; Crianza 2 years with 1 in oak.

Cabernet Franc: primary flavors strawberry, raspberry, bell pepper, crushed gravel, chili pepper; dry, medium body, medium-high tannins, high acidity, 11.5-13.5% ABV; herbaceous bell-pepper aroma from methoxypyrazines; parent of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
Loire Cabernet Franc: cool climate, lighter body and tannins, red fruit, floral and herbal notes. Chinon: roasted red pepper, raspberry, jalapeno, wet gravel; high acidity, moderately low tannin.
Touraine: Chinon and Bourgueil are famous for reds; Bourgueil is listed as Cabernet Franc.
Court grape profile, Merlot: climates moderate, warm; destemming, blending, new oak; top regions Bordeaux, California, Chile; color medium ruby, deep ruby, purple.

Merlot: primary flavors cherry, chocolate, plum, bay leaf, vanilla; medium-full body, medium-high tannins, medium acidity, 13.5-15% ABV; softer and less astringent than Cabernet Sauvignon because of thinner skins and fewer seeds; red plum and cherry in cooler climates, baked blackberry and fruitcake in warmer ones.

US Merlot is generally riper and more fruit-forward than French and Italian; Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon share Cabernet Franc as a parent, so they are half-siblings. Pomerol Merlot: clay-rich soils; concentrated black cherry and plum, subtle truffle, velvety texture. Napa Merlot: full-bodied, velvety, sometimes slightly minty.
Pomerol: red only; Merlot about 80%, Cabernet Franc 15%, Cabernet Sauvignon 5%.
Saint-Emilion, Pomerol and Fronsac (the Right Bank) are shaped by Merlot on limestone plateaus, molasse and clay.
Court grape profile, Cabernet Sauvignon: climates moderate, warm, hot; destemming, blending, new oak; color deep ruby, ruby, purple, dark purple.

Cabernet Sauvignon: primary flavors black cherry, black currant, cedar, baking spices, graphite; dry, full body, medium-high tannins, medium-high acidity, 13.5-15% ABV. Bordeaux: black currant, anise, tobacco leaf, pencil lead, the most savory expressions, mostly blended, best on gravel in the Medoc and Graves. North Coast California: black currant, blackberry, pencil lead, tobacco, mint.
Cabernet Sauvignon shares pyrazines with the other Bordeaux varieties: green peppercorn, graphite or bell pepper notes.
Medoc appellations include Haut-Medoc, Margaux, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Saint-Estephe; the Medoc makes only red wines.
Court: Paso Robles is warm continental with large day-night temperature swings.

Court grape profile, Syrah: climates moderate, warm, hot; styles spicy, savory; blending, large barrel, whole cluster; top regions Northern Rhone (Hermitage, Cote-Rotie, Saint-Joseph) and Barossa (Shiraz); color deep ruby to deep purple/violet.

Syrah: primary flavors blueberry, black plum, milk chocolate, tobacco, green peppercorn; full body, medium-high tannins, medium acidity, 13.5-15% ABV; among the most intensely colored reds; dark fruit, savory notes, a lingering peppery finish. French versions have more acidity and earthy, herbaceous aromas; Australian versions are more fruit-driven with lots of spice.
Barossa Shiraz is among the most powerful in the world, often 14-15% alcohol.
Cornas reds are single-varietal Syrah; Cote-Rotie, Saint-Joseph, Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage allow single-varietal or blends.

Malbec: primary flavors red plum, blackberry, vanilla, sweet tobacco, cocoa; dry, full body, medium tannins, medium-low acidity, 13.5-15% ABV. Thick skins high in color pigment; a classic blind-tasting tell is a bright magenta rim and opaque purple color; it keeps acidity best at high elevations with cold nights.
Court (Certified column): Malbec can have an electric purple color from more sun at higher elevations; Mendoza vineyards are 600-1,200 m.
Court: new or used, French or American oak are all common for Malbec; Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon pair with steak and chimichurri.

Zinfandel: primary flavors blackberry, strawberry, peach preserves, cinnamon, sweet tobacco; dry, medium-full body, medium-high tannins, medium-low acidity, over 15% ABV; jammy fruit and smoky spice; uneven ripening leaves raisined berries that raise alcohol; genetically identical to Croatia's Tribidrag, and called Primitivo in Italy. North Coast: blackberry, black cherry, bramble, vanilla, black pepper. It performs well in warm, sunny regions. White Zinfandel is a sweet rosé from the same grape.

unverified: Typical grape profiles (fruit, tannin, acidity, alcohol) come from Wine Folly, not the Court, and vary by producer and vintage.
The Court's Grape Variety Profiles PDF is image-based. Its colors and climates here come from the Level 1 audit of that PDF (tasting.json, italy.json), not from a fresh read.
Climate and country calls in the grid tiles (e.g. Grenache: warm) are drawn from the Court's profiles and region descriptions, not from a Court answer key.
The Court's sample Australian red grid doesn't name its grape in the text we have; we present it as an Australian example only.
The Gigondas section rests on Inter Rhône's general Southern Rhône facts; no Gigondas-specific source was fetched.
No Wine Folly, Court or official video focused on Gamay or Beaujolais was found, so that grape has no video of its own.

read.bigIdea: Light reds: tell them apart by earth, ripeness and carbonic.
read.where: The Court lists **Pinot Noir** from the **Côte d'Or** (Village or Premier Cru), **California** (Carneros, Sonoma, Central Coast) and Oregon's **Willamette Valley**, and **Gamay** from **Beaujolais**, made **with carbonic maceration** and **no oak**. All four are paler reds with red fruit, low tannin and bright acidity.

stops.name: Burgundy
stops.text: Red fruit with **earthy** and **floral** notes; mushroom and leather come with age. Watch for warm vintages: riper fruit, more oak and **no earth yet** can blur the line between Old and New World.

stops.name: California and Oregon
stops.text: California is **bigger and lusher**: black cherry, cola, vanilla. Oregon is **lighter and tarter** (cranberry, Bing cherry) and often closest to Burgundy. The Willamette Valley is cool, with maritime influence.

stops.name: Beaujolais
stops.text: **Carbonic maceration** gives juicy raspberry and cranberry, **banana** and candied notes, **low tannin** and **high acidity**. Tick the red grid's **carbonic maceration** line.

read.visualIntro: How the four look on the grid:
read.mixup: **Beaujolais** is Gamay, made carbonic. **Red Burgundy** is Pinot Noir, with earth and oak.
read.sayIt: Light and silky, with red cherry and a little earth. Great with salmon or mushrooms.

read.bigIdea: Italy's two: both tart and firm, but Nebbiolo grips harder.
read.where: The exam's **Nebbiolo** is **Barolo** or **Barbaresco**, in Piedmont. Its **Sangiovese** is **Brunello di Montalcino** (100% Sangiovese) or **Chianti Classico** (at least 80%). Both can show **garnet** in the glass.

stops.name: Nebbiolo
stops.text: **Cherry**, **rose**, leather and anise, with **high tannin** and **high acidity**. Color runs medium ruby to **garnet**, often with a garnet or orange rim even young. Barolo ages **38 months** (18 in oak); Barbaresco **26** (9 in oak).

stops.name: Sangiovese
stops.text: **Cherry**, **roasted tomato**, **oregano** and **sweet balsamic**, with medium-high tannin and acidity. The **dried herbs** and **balsamic** lines can both come into play.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: The Court's profiles put Nebbiolo in **moderate to warm** climates and Sangiovese in **warm to hot** ones.

read.mixup: **Barbaresco** has the shorter minimum aging (26 months). **Barolo** needs 38.

read.bigIdea: Grenache: ripe red fruit, dried herbs and warmth.
read.where: The exam's Grenache is **Châteauneuf-du-Pape** or **Gigondas**, in the **Southern Rhône**, where reds are Grenache-based blends. Châteauneuf has a **Mediterranean** climate, the **Mistral** wind and about **2,800 hours** of sunshine a year.

stops.name: Look
stops.text: **Medium to deep ruby**, and often a **garnet or orange rim** even when young.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Stewed strawberry**, **grilled plum** and blood orange, with **leather** and **dried herbs**.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: **Medium tannin**, **medium acidity** and **high alcohol**, often over 15%. The Court's profile puts it in **warm to hot** climates.

read.mixup: **Southern Rhône** reds are Grenache-based. **Northern Rhône** reds are Syrah.

read.bigIdea: Rioja: red fruit, dill and the marks of time.
read.where: The exam's Tempranillo is **Rioja Reserva** or **Gran Reserva**, aged in **American oak**. Rioja is continental, in the rain shadow of the Cantabrian Mountains along the Ebro. Reserva needs **3 years** of aging (1 in oak); Gran Reserva **5 years** (2 in oak).

stops.name: Look
stops.text: **Medium ruby to garnet**: Tempranillo's skins are thin.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Cherry** and **dried fig**, with **cedar**, **tobacco**, **dill** and vanilla. Dill and coconut sit on the red grid's **new oak** line. With 10 to 20 years, dried fruit, nuts and spice take over.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: **Medium-high tannin** and **medium-high acidity**, medium-full body. The Court's profile puts it in **warm to hot** climates.

read.mixup: **Crianza** is the youngest aged tier and isn't on the exam. **Reserva** and **Gran Reserva** are.

keyPoints.line: and Bourgueil: Loire Cabernet Franc, cool and herbal.

Merlot has thinner skins and fewer seeds than Cabernet.

read.bigIdea: Same family: Loire Cab Franc is crisp, Merlot is plush.
read.where: The Court lists **Cabernet Franc** from **Chinon** or **Bourgueil** in the Loire, and **Merlot** from **Pomerol** or **Saint-Émilion** on Bordeaux's Right Bank, plus **Napa** and **Sonoma** with new oak. Cabernet Franc is a **parent** of both Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon.

stops.name: Loire Cabernet Franc
stops.text: **Raspberry**, **roasted red pepper**, **jalapeño** and wet gravel. **High acidity**, moderately **low tannin**, lighter body. The green notes come from **pyrazines**: tick the green bell pepper line.

stops.name: Right Bank Merlot
stops.text: **Black cherry**, **plum**, chocolate and a hint of truffle, with a **velvety** feel. Pomerol is about **80% Merlot**, on clay-rich soils.

stops.name: California Merlot
stops.text: **Full-bodied** and velvety, riper, with new oak and sometimes a **minty** note. Cooler Merlot leans to red plum and cherry; warmer Merlot to baked blackberry.

read.visualIntro: Two family members, side by side:
read.mixup: **Cabernet Franc** is the parent. **Merlot** and **Cabernet Sauvignon** are its offspring (half-siblings).

read.bigIdea: Cabernet: black currant, cedar, and a firm frame.
read.where: The exam's Cabernet Sauvignon is **Bordeaux** (**Haut-Médoc**, **Graves**) or **California** (**Napa**, **Sonoma**, **Paso Robles**), all with **new oak**. In Bordeaux it does best on **gravel** and is mostly **blended**.

stops.name: Bordeaux
stops.text: **Black currant**, **tobacco leaf**, anise and **pencil lead**: Wine Folly calls these the most **savory** Cabernets.

stops.name: California
stops.text: **Black currant**, **blackberry**, pencil lead, tobacco and sometimes **mint**. Paso Robles is warm continental, with big day-night swings.

stops.name: Original vs modern Napa
stops.text: The original style shows **pyrazines** and just-ripe fruit. The modern one has **high alcohol**, rounder tannins, overripe fruit and **more oak**.

read.mixup: **Haut-Médoc** and **Graves** are Left Bank Cabernet country. **Pomerol** and **Saint-Émilion** are Right Bank Merlot country.

read.bigIdea: Syrah: dark fruit and pepper, earthy or ripe.
read.where: The exam's Syrah is **Northern Rhône** (**Côte-Rôtie**, **Saint-Joseph**, **Crozes-Hermitage**) or **Australian Shiraz** from South Australia, Western Australia or Victoria, with **new oak**. Syrah has some of the most intense color of any red.

stops.name: Northern Rhône
stops.text: **Black plum** and **blueberry**, **pepper**, savory and earthy, herbal notes, with **more acidity**.

stops.name: Australia
stops.text: Riper, more fruit-driven, **lots of spice**. Barossa Shiraz often reaches **14-15%** alcohol.

stops.name: The Court's sample
stops.text: The filled-in red grid that concluded **Australia** gave **black fruit**, **black pepper** and **eucalyptus** as its grape reasons, and **high alcohol** and **very ripe fruit** for climate.

read.mixup: **Syrah** and **Shiraz** are the same grape. The name on the label hints at the style.

read.where: The exam's Malbec is from **Mendoza**, Argentina, where vineyards sit at **600-1,200 m**. Malbec's thick skins are rich in color pigment, and the Court notes high-altitude sun can give an **electric purple** color.

stops.name: Look
stops.text: **Opaque purple** with a **bright magenta rim**.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Red plum**, **blackberry**, **cocoa**, **sweet tobacco** and vanilla.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: **Full body**, **medium tannin** and **medium-low acidity**. It keeps acid best at high elevation, with cold nights.

read.mixup: **Malbec** has softer acid and a magenta rim. **Shiraz** shows black pepper and sometimes eucalyptus.
read.sayIt: Plush and dark, with plum and cocoa. Made for steak with chimichurri.

keyPoints.line: with new oak: the exam's Zinfandel.
blackberry and strawberry, sweet spice, tobacco.
alcohol is common; raisined berries add sugar.
medium-low acidity, medium-high tannin.
is the same grape; Croatia's Tribidrag too.

read.bigIdea: Zinfandel: jammy fruit, sweet spice and real heat.
read.where: The exam's Zinfandel is **California**: **Napa Valley** or **Sonoma County**, with **new oak**. Zinfandel ripens unevenly, so **raisined berries** sit beside ripe ones, which concentrates sugar and raises alcohol.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Blackberry**, **strawberry** and peach-preserve jamminess, with **cinnamon** and **sweet tobacco**. North Coast versions add bramble, vanilla and **black pepper**.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: **Medium-high tannin**, **medium-low acidity** and **high alcohol**, often over 15%.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: **United States**. Fruit condition calls like **jammy** or **dried** fit the raisined character.

read.mixup: **Zinfandel** on the exam is a dry red. **White Zinfandel** is a sweet rosé from the same grape.
